props.title: REC
props.initialSlug: Found-footage horror traps reporter in zombie nightmare

sections.content: [REC] (2007) revolutionized found-footage horror by combining claustrophobic apartment building terror with rabies-like infection. Spanish directors Jaume Balagueró and Paco Plaza crafted a masterclass in escalating tension, following a TV reporter and cameraman trapped in a quarantined building. Its influence spawned not just American remake Quarantine (2008), but helped catalyze a wave of Spanish horror including The Orphanage (2007) and Julia's Eyes (2010). The film's documentary-style approach and confined setting created a template for effective low-budget horror that still resonates.

sections.content: The found footage subgenre exploded after The Blair Witch Project (1999), but [REC] (2007) elevated it beyond simple shaky-cam scares. Its use of a professional TV crew provided narrative justification for higher quality footage, while maintaining documentary authenticity. This approach influenced later works like V/H/S (2012) and Trollhunter (2010), which similarly used professional filming contexts to justify their footage quality.

The confined setting of [REC] (2007) taps into a rich tradition of single-location horror, from Night of the Living Dead (1968) to Cube (1997). The apartment building becomes a character itself, with each floor revealing new horrors. This vertical horror concept influenced films like Attack the Block (2011) and The Raid (2011), though those took more action-oriented approaches. SUBHEAD: Spanish Horror Renaissance

sections.content: [REC] (2007) emerged during a golden age of Spanish horror cinema. Directors like Guillermo del Toro with The Devil's Backbone (2001) and Pan's Labyrinth (2006) had already put Spanish genre film on the map. [REC] continued this momentum alongside films like The Orphanage (2007) and Sleep Tight (2011), combining social commentary with visceral scares. This wave influenced international horror, demonstrating how local folklore and social issues could create universal fear.
